title: Standard string functions from string.h
learningObjectives: Explain the language rule and its constraints.
Trace the example and predict its output.
Identify relevant boundary and safety cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: string.h declares functions for null-terminated byte strings and memory blocks. strlen counts characters before the terminator; strcmp compares strings; strcpy and strcat write to destination storage and require sufficient capacity.
understand.whyItMatters: This concept supports correct handling of C data and helps prevent invalid memory access or incorrect program behaviour.
understand.analogy: Think of the construct as a precisely bounded sequence of storage and operations.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's rules for object lifetime, bounds, types or undefined behaviour.

explain.narrative:
string.h declares functions for null-terminated byte strings and memory blocks. strlen counts characters before the terminator; strcmp compares strings; strcpy and strcat write to destination storage and require sufficient capacity.

Always check the types, object bounds and preconditions required by the operation. Compile with warnings enabled and test ordinary as well as boundary inputs.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.code: Library calls do not prove destination capacity automatically. The programmer must ensure valid source strings, sufficient destination space and compliance with overlap rules.

practise.guidedTask: The capacity check reserves space for both strings and the final null character before strcat appends. The output is C language basics.
practise.independentTask: Calculate both string lengths and the required destination capacity before concatenation.
hints: Compare two input strings using strcmp and explain why equality is tested with == 0.
strcmp returns zero for equal strings, negative for less-than and positive for greater-than.
strncpy may leave the destination unterminated when the source fills the limit.
